---
title: "Polling Simulation Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Polling Simulation activity, which simulates polls of different sizes to demonstrate sampling variability.

## Creating a TRUE/FALSE column with `%in%`

```
ces <- ces |>
  mutate(unaffiliated = trad %in% c("Atheist", "Agnostic", "Nothing in Particular"))
```

`%in%` checks whether each value in the `trad` column matches *any* of the values in the list on the right. If a respondent's `trad` value is "Atheist", "Agnostic", or "Nothing in Particular", the new column gets TRUE; otherwise FALSE. This is cleaner than writing `trad == "Atheist" | trad == "Agnostic" | trad == "Nothing in Particular"`.

## Calculating a proportion from TRUE/FALSE

```
proportion <- mean(ces$unaffiliated)
```

When you take the `mean()` of a TRUE/FALSE column, R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0. So the mean is the proportion of TRUE values. If 35% of respondents are unaffiliated, `mean()` returns 0.35.

## Sampling rows with `sample_n()`

```
sample_50 <- ces |> sample_n(50)
```

`sample_n(50)` randomly picks 50 rows from the data frame. Each run gives different rows unless you set a seed first with `set.seed()`. This simulates drawing a poll sample from the population.

## Writing a simulation function

```
simulate_polls <- function(data, sample_size, n_simulations = 1000) {
  proportions <- replicate(n_simulations, {
    s <- data |> sample_n(sample_size)
    mean(s$unaffiliated)
  })
  tibble(proportion = proportions, sample_size = sample_size)
}
```

This function draws many random samples and records the proportion from each one. Breaking it down:

- `function(data, sample_size, n_simulations = 1000)` defines three inputs. `n_simulations = 1000` is a default — if you do not specify it, it uses 1000.
- `replicate(n_simulations, { ... })` runs the code inside the braces `n_simulations` times and collects all the results into a vector. It is like a for loop that automatically gathers results.
- Inside the braces: sample rows, calculate the proportion. Each repetition returns one number.
- `tibble(...)` packages the results into a data frame at the end.

## Combining data frames with `bind_rows()`

```
simulations_all <- bind_rows(simulations_50, simulations_500) |>
  mutate(sample_size = paste("n =", sample_size))
```

`bind_rows()` stacks two data frames on top of each other — all rows from the first, then all rows from the second. The columns must have the same names. `paste("n =", sample_size)` converts the number 50 into the text "n = 50" for nicer chart labels.

## Side-by-side histograms with `facet_wrap()`

```
ggplot(simulations_all, aes(x = proportion)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = proportion, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sample_size)
```

`facet_wrap(~sample_size)` splits the chart into panels, one per unique value of `sample_size`. Both panels share the same x-axis scale, making it easy to compare the spread of the two distributions. `bins = 30` controls how many bars the histogram uses. `linewidth` is the newer name for what used to be called `size` in `geom_vline()`.

## Common mistakes

**Forgetting `set.seed()` before sampling:**

```
# Different every time you run it:
sample_50 <- ces |> sample_n(50)

# Same result every time (reproducible):
set.seed(42)
sample_50 <- ces |> sample_n(50)
```

Without `set.seed()`, you get different random rows each run. This is fine for exploration, but if your answers need to match someone else's (like a grader's), set the seed.

**Using `==` instead of `%in%` for multiple values:**

```
# Wrong — only checks the first value:
trad == c("Atheist", "Agnostic", "Nothing in Particular")

# Correct — checks if trad matches ANY of the values:
trad %in% c("Atheist", "Agnostic", "Nothing in Particular")
```

`==` with a vector does element-wise comparison (recycling), which gives wrong results. `%in%` checks membership — "is this value anywhere in the list?"

**Confusing `bind_rows()` with `inner_join()`:**

```
# bind_rows() stacks data frames VERTICALLY (adds more rows):
bind_rows(df1, df2)

# inner_join() combines data frames HORIZONTALLY (adds more columns):
inner_join(df1, df2, by = "shared_column")
```

Use `bind_rows()` when your data frames have the same columns and you want to combine them. Use `inner_join()` when they share a key column and you want to merge matching rows side by side.
